The lines were fallen unto Judah in pleasant places, and the bounds of their habitation were the appointment of the same God who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). Shaaraim stands as a witness that no town of the lowland is too small to bear the marks of His salvation.

etymology: Hebrew gederoth, “sheepfolds” or “walls,” a town of the lowland of Judah, later taken by the Philistines in the days of Ahaz.
biblical_def: Gederoth was a town of the Shephelah, the low country of Judah, named in the catalogue of the cities of Judah’s allotment when Joshua divided the land by lot (Jos 15:41). Its name signifies sheepfolds or walls, a fit name for a town set among the pasture-lands of the lowland. In the evil reign of Ahaz, when the LORD humbled Judah for the king’s transgressions, the Philistines invaded the cities of the low country and the south, and Gederoth was among the towns they took and dwelt in (2Ch 28:18). So a town of the inheritance was for a season lost through the sin of an unfaithful king. The dictionary does not labour to fix its exact ruins; what it honours is that the LORD set this little town among the goodly heritage He measured out to His people, and that even its loss preached the truth that sin brings forth the spoiling of the heritage. Gederoth witnesses that the portion the LORD gives must be kept by faith and obedience.

etymology: Hebrew gallim, “heaps” or “springs,” a town near Gibeah of Benjamin, the home of Phalti to whom Saul gave David’s wife Michal.
biblical_def: Gallim was a town that lay near Gibeah in the territory of Benjamin, north of Jerusalem, and though it stood not in the lowland proper it belonged to the same cluster of southern towns whose names Scripture preserves. Its name signifies heaps or springs. It is remembered first because Phalti the son of Laish, “which was of Gallim,” was the man to whom Saul gave Michal, David’s wife, when the king sought to wound David in his absence (1Sa 25:44). Later the prophet Isaiah named Gallim in his vision of the Assyrian’s march upon Jerusalem, when the towns of Benjamin trembled and he cried, “Lift up thy voice, O daughter of Gallim” (Isa 10:30). The dictionary does not labour to fix its exact ruins; what it honours is that the LORD set this little town among the goodly heritage of His people, and made it a witness both to the troubling of His saints and to His warning against the proud invader. The lines were fallen unto Benjamin in pleasant places, and the bounds of their habitation were the appointment of the same God who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). Gallim stands as a witness that the LORD numbers and remembers even the small towns through which His purposes pass.

etymology: Hebrew giloh, perhaps “exile” or “rejoicing,” a town in the hill country of Judah, the home of Ahithophel, David’s counsellor who turned traitor.
biblical_def: Giloh was a town in the hill country of Judah, named in the catalogue of the cities of Judah’s allotment when Joshua divided the land by lot (Jos 15:51). Though it stood in the highlands rather than the lowland proper, it belonged to the same southern inheritance of Judah whose towns Scripture preserves. It is chiefly remembered as the home of Ahithophel the Gilonite, David’s wise counsellor, whose counsel was as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God, and who yet turned traitor and joined Absalom’s conspiracy. “And Absalom sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David’s counsellor, from his city, even from Giloh” (2Sa 15:12). So a quiet town of Judah became the dwelling of one whose treachery prefigured a darker betrayal yet to come. The dictionary does not labour to fix its exact ruins; what it honours is that the LORD set this town among the goodly heritage of His people, and that even the betrayer’s city served the unfolding of His sovereign purpose. The lines were fallen unto Judah in pleasant places, and the bounds of their habitation were the appointment of the same God who divided to the nations their inheritance (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). Giloh witnesses that the LORD reigns even over the counsels of traitors.

etymology: Hebrew chalchul, perhaps “trembling” or “full of hollows,” a town in the hill country of Judah near Hebron, named in the tribal allotment.
biblical_def: Halhul was a town in the hill country of Judah, named in the catalogue of the cities of Judah’s allotment when Joshua divided the land by lot (Jos 15:58). Though it stood in the highlands above the lowland, it belonged to the same southern inheritance of Judah whose towns Scripture preserves, and it lay near Hebron and Beth-zur among the upland cities. Its name has been read as “trembling” or as a place full of hollows. It is named once only in the holy page, among the cities reckoned to this part of Judah’s portion, and no later story is told of it in Scripture. The dictionary does not labour to fix its precise ruins nor to settle the doubtful sense of its name; what it honours is that the LORD numbered even this barely-spoken upland town among the goodly heritage He measured out to His people. The lines were fallen unto Judah in pleasant places, and the bounds of their habitation were the appointment of the same God who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people (Deu 32:8; Act 17:26). Halhul stands as a witness that no portion of the saint’s heritage is too small or too silent for the care of Him who apportioned it.
